blocks.text: “He was almost recovered, but he has been greatly upset by Mr. Hawkins’s death.” He interrupted:—
“Oh, yes, I know, I know. I have read your last two letters.” I went on:—
“I suppose this upset him. When we were in town last Thursday, he had a sort of shock.”
“A shock, and after brain fever so soon! That was not good. What kind of a shock was it?”

“He thought he saw someone who reminded him of something terrible. It was something that had led to his brain fever.” At that moment, the whole thing seemed to overwhelm me all at once. I felt such pity for Jonathan, and I thought of the horror he had experienced. I thought of the whole terrible mystery of his diary, and of the dark fear that has hung over me ever since. All these feelings rushed over me in great confusion. I suppose I lost control of my emotions. I threw myself on my knees, held up my hands to him, and begged him to make my husband well again. He took my hands and helped me stand up. Then he made me sit on the sofa and sat down beside me. He held my hand in his, and spoke to me with such endless kindness:

“My life is an empty and lonely one. It is so full of work that I have not had much time for friendships. Because of this, I have felt the loneliness of my life growing as I get older. But since my friend John Seward called me here, I have met so many good people and seen such noble character. Now I feel that loneliness more than ever. Believe me, then, that I come here full of respect for you. You have given me hope. It is not hope in the matter I am investigating. It is hope that there are still good women left to make life happy. Their lives and their honesty can be a good lesson for the children of the future. I am so glad that I may be of some use to you here. If your husband is suffering, his trouble lies within the area of my study and experience. I promise you that I will gladly do everything I can for him. I will do all I can to make his life strong and brave like a man's, and to make your life happy. Now you must eat. You are exhausted from worry and perhaps too anxious. Your husband Jonathan would not like to see you so pale. When a man sees something upsetting in the person he loves, it is not good for him. So, for his sake, you must eat and smile. You have told me all about Lucy. We will not speak of that now, so that it does not upset you. I will stay in Exeter tonight. I want to think carefully about what you have told me. When I have thought about it, I will ask you some questions, if I may. Then you will also tell me as much as you can about your husband Jonathan’s trouble, but not yet. You must eat now. Afterwards, you will tell me everything.”
After lunch, we went back to the sitting room, and he said to me:

“And now tell me all about him.” When the moment came to speak to this great, wise man, I began to feel afraid. That journal is all so strange. I feared he would think that I was a weak fool, and that Jonathan was a madman. I hesitated to go on. But he was so sweet and kind, and he had promised to help. I trusted him, so I said:

“Dr. Van Helsing, what I have to tell you is so strange that you must not laugh at me or at my husband. Since yesterday, my mind has been burning with doubt. You must be kind to me. Please do not think I am foolish because I have even half believed some very strange things.” Both his manner and his words comforted me when he said:

“Oh, my dear, if you only knew how strange the matter is that brought me here, you would be the one to laugh. I have learned not to look down on anyone’s belief, no matter how strange it is. I have tried to keep an open mind. Ordinary things in life could not close my mind. Neither could strange and extraordinary things, even the things that make a person doubt whether they are mad or sane.”
